questions.q: Define net force and state its SI unit. If two forces of 10 N and 15 N act on a box in the same direction, what is the net force?
questions.a: Net force is the vector sum of all forces acting on an object; its SI unit is newton (N). For forces in the same direction, net force = 10 N + 15 N = 25 N in that direction. A wrong answer (e.g., 5 N or 150 N) reveals the student is either subtracting instead of adding, or multiplying magnitudes, showing they do not grasp that forces in the same direction add as scalars with direction.

questions.q: Two students push a heavy desk: one pushes north with 30 N, the other pushes south with 45 N. Explain why the net force is 15 N south, not 75 N or 15 N north.
questions.a: Forces are vectors; opposite directions mean we subtract magnitudes (45 N - 30 N = 15 N) and the direction follows the larger force (south). A wrong answer of 75 N shows the student added magnitudes ignoring direction (treating forces as scalars). An answer of 15 N north reveals they subtracted correctly but assigned the direction of the smaller force, misunderstanding that the net force points in the direction of the larger force.

questions.q: A boat is pulled by two ropes: one exerts 20 N east, the other exerts 15 N north. Calculate the magnitude of the net force on the boat. (Use Pythagoras: √(20² + 15²))
questions.a:
Step 1: Identify perpendicular forces: F₁ = 20 N east, F₂ = 15 N north.
Step 2: Net force magnitude = √(F₁² + F₂²) = √(20² + 15²) = √(400 + 225) = √625 = 25 N.
Step 3: Direction is northeast (at an angle tan⁻¹(15/20) ≈ 37° north of east).
A wrong answer of 35 N indicates scalar addition (20+15). An answer of 5 N indicates scalar subtraction. Both show the student cannot apply vector addition for perpendicular forces.

questions.q: Analyze the following free-body diagram: a block on a smooth floor has three horizontal forces: 10 N →, 6 N ←, and 4 N →. Compare the net force to a situation where only a single 8 N → force acts. Are the effects on the block's motion identical? Why?
questions.a: Yes, the effects are identical. Net force in first case: (10 + 4) → + 6 ← = 14 → - 6 ← = 8 N →. This matches the single 8 N → force. Since net force determines acceleration (Newton's Second Law), identical net forces produce identical acceleration. A "No" answer reveals the student thinks the number of forces matters more than their vector sum, or they incorrectly calculated the net force as 20 N or 2 N.

questions.q: A classmate argues: "If three forces act on an object — 5 N up, 5 N down, and 10 N right — the net force is 20 N because you add all the magnitudes." Evaluate this statement and correct the error.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. Vertical forces (5 N up and 5 N down) cancel each other (net vertical force = 0 N). The horizontal force (10 N right) remains. Net force = 10 N right, not 20 N. The error is adding magnitudes of forces in different directions without vector addition. A student who agrees reveals they treat force as a scalar quantity, ignoring that opposite forces cancel and perpendicular forces combine via Pythagoras.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using spring balances and a small ring to demonstrate that two perpendicular forces of 3 N and 4 N produce a net force of 5 N. Describe the setup, measurements, and how you would verify the resultant magnitude and direction.
questions.a: Setup: Tie three strings to a small ring. Attach two spring balances to two strings, pulling horizontally at 90° (e.g., east and north) with 3 N and 4 N respectively. Attach a third spring balance to the third string and pull in the opposite direction (southwest) until the ring is centered (equilibrium). The third balance reads 5 N, confirming the resultant of 3 N and 4 N is 5 N. Direction is along the third string. A poor answer omits the equilibrium condition or uses only two balances, showing they don't understand that the net force is balanced by an equal and opposite force for verification.
